name: Shambala
sweep_summary: Shambala (sham1280) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant penultimate, decided by Steere 1867 ('The Accent in Shambala words invariably falls upon the last syllable but one'; quote re-verified, but the page is p.4 by the scanned page headers, not p.2). The two title-keyword items are both by Philippson: the 1991/92 Paris 5 thesis (Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale) is a ~30-language comparative overview whose theses.fr abstract describes a continuum from tonal to demarcative-penultimate-stress systems and does not name Shambaa; it has no online full text (theses.fr 'accessible: non', no HAL, no OA PDF) - relevance unclear, priority medium. The 2005 paper (Pitch accent in Comorian and Proto-Sabaki tones, RMCA Tervuren volume) is about Comorian/Proto-Sabaki, not Shambaa (Seuta, G23): other-language, print-only, priority low. A side find, Philippson 1998 (Faits de Langues, Persée, doi 10.3406/flang.1998. Files already on file from the earlier catalog audit were re-read: Odden 1982 SAL 13(2):179 gives the best first-hand statement - penultimate syllable stressed, realized as vowel lengthening with no pitch change - and supersedes Steere 1867 as deciding source; Seidel 1895 §4 p.1 ('Der Wortton ruht stets auf der vorletzten Silbe', stress shifts with suffixation, stressed open vowels long) and Riedel 2009 pp.17-20 (second-hand from Odden) confirm; Mndeme & Ligembe 2022 has a penultimate-vowel-lengthening rule but no stress statement. Catalog coding confirmed; deciding source should move to Odden 1982:179. lookups went through theses.fr, HAL, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, archive.org and Persée APIs (OpenAlex, Google Books and HathiTrust were quota- or challenge-blocked).

new_statements.quote: It should also be noted that the penultimate syllable of a word is stressed, realized phonetically as a lengthening of the penultimate vowel (but with no perceivable changes in pitch). A lengthened penultimate vowel is shorter than a long vowel, so the unstressed long vowel in ku-kaang-iy-a 'to fry for' is longer than the stressed vowel i. A stressed long vowel becomes even longer, so that the penultimate vowel in aa-ghook-a 'he is standing' is longer than the unstressed vowel aa.
new_statements.citation: Odden, David (1982). Tonal phenomena in KiShambaa. Studies in African Linguistics 13(2): 177-208.
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress, cued by vowel duration (penultimate lengthening) and not by pitch; tone (H/L with downstep) is a separate system. First-hand 1981 field data from a native speaker (eastern dialect). Agrees with the catalog's fixed-dominant penultimate coding (rule_v3 '10 010 0010 00010') and with Seidel 1895 §4 and Steere 1867; adds the phonetic characterization and the stress/tone independence.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (128-page full-issue scan of SAL 13(2), 1982). The passage is on PDF page 91, whose running header reads "Tonal Phenomena in KiShambaa 179"; I rendered the page image and read it directly. The printed prose matches the reported quotation word for word, from "It should also be noted that the penultimate syllable of a word is stressed..." to "... is longer than the unstressed vowel áá." audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant penult' rests on Steere 1867 p.2, a one-sentence remark in a missionary primer; we held no copy, but the archive.org text fetched sources now confirms the sentence verbatim at p.2. The coding itself is safe: Odden 1982 (SAL 13.2, p.179), the standard phonological description of KiShambaa, states that the penultimate syllable of every word is stressed, realized as sub-phonemic lengthening (distinct from the marginal lexical length contrast) with no pitch correlate; Seidel 1895 p.1 says the same and adds that stress shifts with suffixation; Riedel 2009 and Mndeme & Ligembe 2022 repeat it; Hyman 2009/2013 (already held under other glottocodes) quote Odden 1999:192-3 to the same effect. Nothing found suggests exceptions or a non-penult pattern. Recommended: keep kind=fixed-dominant/penult, swap or add Odden 1982:179 as the deciding citation (phonology article, fieldwork 1981)

sources.citation: Steere 1867, Collections for a Handbook of the Shambala Language, p.2, archive.org full text (sole accent statement; no exceptions given)
sources.quote: The Accent in Shambala words invariably falls upon the last syllable but one.

sources.citation: Odden, David (1982). Tonal phenomena in KiShambaa. Studies in African Linguistics 13(2): 177-208.
sources.quote: It should also be noted that the penultimate syllable of a word is stressed, realized phonetically as a lengthening of the penultimate vowel (but with no perceivable changes in pitch). A lengthened penultimate vowel is shorter than a long vowel, so the unstressed long vowel in ku-kaang-iy-a 'to fry for' is longer than the stressed vowel i. A stressed long vowel becomes even longer, so that the penultimate vowel in aa-ghook-a 'he is standing' is longer than the unstressed vowel aa.
sources.locator: p.179, section 2 'Phonetic Problems' (scanned text layer; obvious scanned noise normalized)
sources.note: First-hand (1981 fieldwork, eastern dialect, speaker from Tanga): word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable, realized as penultimate vowel lengthening with no perceptible pitch change; tone (H/L + downstep) is independent of stress. The paper also uses a [-stress] condition on object prefixes in its tonal rules (pp. ~194-198), i.e. stress is treated as a real phonological property.

sources.citation: Riedel, Kristina (2009). The Syntax of Object Marking in Sambaa: A comparative Bantu perspective. LOT Dissertation Series 213. Utrecht: LOT (Leiden PhD).
sources.quote: "There is no phonemic vowel length alternation. The vowel of the penultimate syllable of a word is lengthened in Sambaa (Odden 1982)..." and "According to Odden (1982), Sambaa has regular penultimate stress. He argues that this is expressed by lengthening the penultimate vowel, not by pitch raising." (second-hand, cites Odden)
sources.note: Second-hand (citing Odden 1982): regular penultimate stress realized as penultimate lengthening, not pitch raising.

sources.citation: Seidel, August. 1895. Handbuch der Shambala-Sprache in Usambara, Deutsch-Ostafrika. Dresden & Leipzig: A. Koehler. (archive.org id bub_gb_ANTfAAAAMAAJ)
sources.quote: "Der Wortton ruht stets auf der vorletzten Silbe, z. B. muhha. Treten Wortbildungs- oder Flexionssilben an ein Wort, so aendert sich danach die Betonung, z. B. muhitai." (stress always on the penult and shifts rightward when suffixes are added)
sources.note: Stress is always penultimate and shifts with suffixation; stressed open-syllable vowels are long (the same lengthening Odden describes).

sources.citation: Steere, Edward. 1867. Collections for a Handbook of the Shambala Language. Zanzibar: Central African Mission Press. (archive.org id collectionsfora00steegoog)
sources.quote: "The Accent in Shambala words invariably falls upon the last syllable but one."
sources.note: Sole accent statement: invariably penultimate; no exceptions given. Re-read: quote verified verbatim; the page locator in the catalog (p.2) looks off by two pages.

sources.citation: Mndeme, Anuarite Samwel & Nestory Nyamwala Ligembe. 2022. Phonological Processes of Shambaa. International Journal of English Literature and Social Sciences 7(3): 41-61. doi:10.22161/ijels.73.8
sources.quote: Treats penultimate vowel lengthening (PVL) as a regular automatic process of Shambaa ordered after segmental rules; no separate stress statement. Low-tier journal, native-speaker fieldwork in Lushoto.
sources.note: Treats 'penultimate vowel lengthening (PVL)' as a regular Shambaa rule (e.g. /mioyo/ -> [myo:yo], /ndema/ -> [nde:ma]) but never states stress placement for Shambaa (its only 'penultimate stress' sentence is about English, citing Chomsky & Halle). Consistent with penultimate stress-as-lengthening; silent on stress itself.

[...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems. // FR: Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. [...] l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.locator: theses.fr record, FR and EN abstracts; field "accessible": "non"
sources.note: Comparative overview of the prosodic systems of ~30 East African Bantu languages, from purely tonal (Kikuyu) to purely demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili); argues the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent drove the evolution of these systems. The abstract does not name Shambaa/G23, so whether it contains a Shambaa-specific stress statement could not be verified. No online full text: theses.fr marks it not accessible; no HAL record (author search, 16 records, none this thesis); Semantic Scholar record has no OA PDF; Google Books/OpenAlex lookups failed on quota.
